word_order: SVO — the sample repeatedly shows subjects before verbs and objects/complements after them, e.g. "Plants make their food" and "Blogs can also help improve student writing."
register: written expository prose / encyclopedia-style explanatory text
target_language_risks: English often delays the main predicate with relative clauses, participial phrases, and parentheticals, so splitting too early can leave Korean without the verb needed to resolve the clause.
Pronouns like it, this, that, they, and one often depend on prior context and should not be isolated from their antecedents.
Lists and coordinated predicates may look segmentable, but in Korean the full connective relation is often needed before translating naturally.
notes_for_prompt_writer: Prefer splitting at strong clause boundaries signaled by comma plus discourse marker or subordinator, but keep embedded relatives and short modifying phrases attached to the noun or clause they modify. Do not start a segment with closing punctuation; attach commas, periods, closing quotes, and closing parentheses to the preceding unit. When an English clause contains a delayed main verb or a pronoun whose referent appears earlier, wait until that context is available before emitting the segment.
